clue.text: Source of victory in the Louvre

definitions.text: Source of victory in the Louvre

parts.words: Source of victory in the Louvre
parts.note: the Winged Victory statue in the Louvre is named after the Aegean island where it was dug up, so the 'source' is a place, not a cause

explanation.surface: A question about what brings success in a Paris gallery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Victory' looks abstract, but it is the Winged Victory, the Greek statue of Nike in the Louvre, named after the island where it was found.
explanation.definitionFit: The Nike statue in the Louvre was found on this northern Aegean island in 1863, hence its full title.

clue.text: Farm boy among Flora Poste's ethical problems

indicators.note: the farm boy is found among the letters of the words that follow, running across the join

explanation.surface: A farmhand caught up in the moral dilemmas of the heroine of Cold Comfort Farm.
explanation.walkthrough: Flora Poste is the heroine of Stella Gibbons's Cold Comfort Farm; the Starkadder farm boy there is Seth, so the answer fits the surface too.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cold Comfort Farm the brooding young Starkadder who works the land is called by this name, a literal boy of the farm.

clue.text: Vidal's Mary, quite contrary

definitions.note: the definition is a possessive standing for the title character of a Gore Vidal novel

indicators.note: from the nursery rhyme 'Mary, Mary, quite contrary', here telling us to turn the name's letters about

explanation.surface: Gore Vidal's version of the nursery-rhyme Mary is a contrary one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quite contrary' is lifted from the nursery rhyme, but here it rearranges the four letters of Mary.
explanation.definitionFit: Myra Breckinridge is Gore Vidal's 1968 novel, its title character being the possession named by 'Vidal's'.

clue.text: The notes on clan reveal racy tales

parts.note: D and E are both musical notes
Cameron is a Scottish Highland clan

explanation.surface: Musical notes about a Scottish clan expose some saucy stories.
explanation.definitionFit: Boccaccio's fourteenth-century collection of a hundred stories, many of them bawdy, told by young Florentines escaping plague.

clue.text: Valued, like promoted seaman in O Brian Soviet minister in company with maiden girl on a river

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Valued, like promoted seaman in O Brian Soviet minister in company with maiden girl on a river (5)', has 5-down's clue run into it; the true clue is the first part only and there is no scan to repair it from.
annotationWithheld.clue: Valued, like promoted seaman in O Brian Soviet minister in company with maiden girl on a river

clue.text: Soviet minister in company with maiden girl on a river

parts.note: M stands for a maiden over in cricket scoring
a miss is a girl or young unmarried woman
R is the map abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A Soviet official is out with a young woman by a river.
explanation.walkthrough: M for maiden comes from cricket, where a maiden over (no runs conceded) is marked M on the scorecard.
explanation.definitionFit: Before 1946 the heads of Soviet government departments were styled people's commissars, the equivalent of ministers.

clue.text: "The gentleman talked —, the ladies laughed and were angry" (Oliver Goldsmith, Citizen of the World)

definitions.text: "The gentleman talked —, the ladies laughed and were angry" (Oliver Goldsmith, Citizen of the World)

parts.words: "The gentleman talked —, the ladies laughed and were angry" (Oliver Goldsmith, Citizen of the World)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: the missing word is the kind of indecent talk that would make eighteenth-century ladies both laugh and take offence

explanation.surface: A line from Goldsmith's satirical letters with one word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Supply the word Goldsmith used for the gentleman's improper talk; the ladies' mixed reaction of laughter and anger points to something obscene.
explanation.definitionFit: Indecent or obscene talk is called filth or dirt, and the missing word is the short term for it.

clue.text: Horse by tree leads us to novel diplomat

parts.note: a mount is a horse for riding
the olive is a tree

explanation.surface: A horse standing by a tree guides us to a fictional envoy.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition covers both the Durrell novel and its title character, the British ambassador in Egypt.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawrence Durrell's third Alexandria Quartet novel is named after its hero, a British ambassador.

clue.text: NBC are destroyed in story describing tent

indicators.note: to describe a shape is to draw round it, so the story wraps round the other letters

parts.note: a tale is a story

indicators.note: the letters of the TV network and 'are' are wrecked and rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: An American TV network's programme being wrecked by a news story about a tent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'describing' puts BERNAC (the anagram of NBC ARE, from 'destroyed') inside TALE.
explanation.definitionFit: The portable sanctuary the Israelites carried through the wilderness was a large tent, and the word still means a tent or booth.

clue.text: Ben Travers suggesting moment for dramatic flop?

definitions.meaning: the definition is the author standing for one of his Aldwych farces
a theatrical failure is a turkey, and a moment is a time

explanation.surface: The farce writer Ben Travers seems to hint at the moment a play bombs.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben Travers wrote a run of Aldwych farces in the 1920s and 1930s, one of them titled with this phrase; 'turkey' is theatre slang for a flop.
explanation.definitionFit: Travers's 1931 farce bears this title, and read literally it names the hour when a show is a failure.

clue.text: Speechless preceding Margaret Avison's founding

definitions.meaning: placed in front of 'founding' this word makes the title of Margaret Avison's 1966 poetry collection

explanation.surface: Someone struck silent ahead of the launch of a poet's enterprise.
explanation.walkthrough: Margaret Avison was a Canadian poet whose collection The Dumbfounding appeared in 1966.
explanation.definitionFit: Mute and voiceless both describe someone without speech, and the word set before 'founding' gives Avison's title.

clue.text: Eliot's women spoke of him

parts.note: in Prufrock the women come and go in the room talking of a Renaissance artist

explanation.surface: A man who was the topic of gossip among women in Eliot.
explanation.walkthrough: The reference is the refrain of T. S. Eliot's 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock': 'In the room the women come and go / Talking of' the Sistine Chapel painter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Renaissance sculptor and painter is the subject of the women's chatter in Eliot's Prufrock refrain.

clue.text: Nabokov's work taking ominous turn?

parts.note: a bend is a turn in a road or river
sinister means threatening or ominous

explanation.surface: A Nabokov book takes a dark and menacing direction.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives 'ominous' before 'turn', but the pieces go in answer order; the title is also a heraldic term for a diagonal band.
explanation.definitionFit: Nabokov's 1947 novel about a philosopher under a totalitarian state carries this heraldic title.

clue.text: Ways to good item from Sitwell collection

parts.note: streets are ways or roads
'to' and 'on' are interchangeable in phrases like 'push the door to', meaning against or onward

explanation.surface: Routes leading to something fine from a poet's anthology.
explanation.walkthrough: Edith Sitwell's 1942 collection was called Street Songs, so one poem from it is a single item of that name.
explanation.definitionFit: Sitwell's wartime volume Street Songs gives its name to each of its poems, ballads of the kind sung on the street.

clue.text: The Man that Corrupted Hadleyburg

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'The Man that Corrupted Hadleyburg (10)', is Mark Twain's story title and does not define or build STEPHENSON; the real clue is missing and there is no scan or reprint.

clue.text: Her tracts loosely concern subordinate princes

indicators.note: loosely means the letters of the two words are held together freely and rearranged

explanation.surface: A woman's pamphlets have a bearing on minor royalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loosely' rearranges the nine letters of HER TRACTS.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Roman Empire a ruler of a quarter of a province, such as Herod Antipas, was a minor prince under Rome.

clue.text: Fowles's acquisitive type finds Hannibal on mountain pass

indicators.note: 'on' here means after, so the cannibal's surname is added to the end of the pass

parts.note: a col is a pass between mountain peaks
Hannibal Lecter is Thomas Harris's cannibal psychiatrist; the clue uses the -OR spelling of the surname, as in the 1986 film Manhunter's Lecktor

explanation.surface: Hannibal crossing the Alps by a mountain pass, as a hoarder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hannibal' with a mountain pass suggests the Carthaginian general crossing the Alps, but it is Hannibal Lecter; the setter spells the surname LECTOR to fit.
explanation.definitionFit: John Fowles's 1963 novel is about a butterfly hoarder who captures a young woman, so its title figure is acquisitive by nature.

clue.text: Hartley's anemone symbolized her

parts.note: in L. P. Hartley's novel the sea creature that eats the shrimp stands for the domineering elder sister

explanation.surface: A flower in a novel stands for a particular woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anemone' looks like the flower, but in L. P. Hartley's The Shrimp and the Anemone it is the sea anemone: Eustace is the shrimp and his bossy sister is the anemone.
explanation.definitionFit: Eustace's older sister in Hartley's trilogy is the anemone of the first title, which devours the shrimp.

clue.text: English, very quiet, that is Eliot's adopted child

parts.note: pp, pianissimo, is the musical mark for very quiet
i.e., id est, means that is

explanation.surface: A very quiet English child adopted in a George Eliot story.
explanation.walkthrough: Here 'Eliot' is George Eliot: in Silas Marner the weaver adopts a foundling girl.
explanation.definitionFit: The golden-haired foundling Silas Marner raises in George Eliot's novel is given this pet name.

clue.text: He "stood at his castle gate / A combing his milk-white steed"

definitions.text: He "stood at his castle gate / A combing his milk-white steed"

parts.words: He "stood at his castle gate / A combing his milk-white steed"
parts.note: the opening lines of an old English ballad about a nobleman who leaves his love and returns to find her dead

explanation.surface: A nobleman grooming his white horse at the gate of his castle.
explanation.walkthrough: The lines open the traditional ballad of that title, Child Ballad 75, in which the lord rides away and comes back to find Lady Nancy Belle dead.
explanation.definitionFit: The ballad's hero, a lord who grooms his horse at his gate before travelling, gives the ballad its name.

clue.text: Greene's stand-up characters?

definitions.meaning: the definition is the possessive standing for a Graham Greene novel
people who do stand-up are comics, so stand-up characters are entertainers

explanation.surface: Graham Greene's characters as comics who stand and tell jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: Graham Greene's 1966 novel, set in Haiti under Papa Doc, bears this title; read literally it describes stand-up comics.
explanation.definitionFit: Greene's Haiti novel takes this title, which plainly means comics who perform stand-up routines.

clue.text: Likeness that is a cover for small magazine

indicators.note: the abbreviation for 'that is' wraps around the short magazine like a cover

parts.note: i.e., id est, means that is
mag is the short form of magazine

explanation.surface: A portrait used as the cover of a little magazine.
explanation.definitionFit: A picture or representation is a likeness of its subject.

clue.text: US soldiers in filmed French novel

parts.note: GI is the standard name for an American soldier, and the plural gives two of them
the second GI from the plural soldiers

explanation.surface: American servicemen appearing in a French novel that became a film.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural 'soldiers' gives two GIs side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Colette's 1944 novella about a Parisian girl raised to be a courtesan was filmed as a 1958 musical.

clue.text: 16's would be rare indeed

parts.note: the cross-reference points to the entry for someone who acquires things; the thing that person prizes is by definition rare

explanation.surface: Something belonging to the entry at 16 would be scarce.
explanation.walkthrough: 16 is the Fowles answer, the hoarder; the phrase 'a 16's piece' names something highly prized because it is scarce.
explanation.definitionFit: A rare piece sought by enthusiasts is a 'collector's' one, so this is the thing in that phrase.

clue.text: Very large South American mountain in Greece

parts.note: OS stands for outsize, a clothing label for very large

explanation.surface: A huge South American peak turns out to be in Greece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very large' is a size label: OS, outsize. The mountain is the one the giants piled on Pelion in myth.
explanation.definitionFit: A peak in Thessaly that the giants stacked on Pelion, in Greek myth, to storm Olympus.

clue.text: A calling for a beau in Augustan comedy

definitions.text: A calling for a beau in Augustan comedy

parts.words: A calling for a beau in Augustan comedy
parts.note: Farquhar's comedy The Beaux' Stratagem has two young men scheming to marry money, so their trade is that of a planner of stratagems

explanation.surface: A suitable profession for a dandy in an eighteenth-century play.
explanation.walkthrough: The play is George Farquhar's 1707 comedy The Beaux' Stratagem; a beau whose business is a stratagem would have this calling.
explanation.definitionFit: A deviser of stratagems, or planner of schemes, is the one whose occupation suits the plotting beaux of Farquhar's title.

clue.text: Cast away weapon, say

indicators.note: 'say' signals that the word for a weapon is spoken, giving a name that sounds the same

parts.note: a gun is a weapon

explanation.surface: Someone tells you to throw a weapon away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast away' reads as an instruction, but it is the castaway Ben Gunn, marooned on the island in Stevenson's Treasure Island.
explanation.definitionFit: Stevenson's marooned pirate Ben in Treasure Island is the island's castaway, left there three years.

clue.text: Route I possibly take (in baby-carriage) to general's tent

indicators.note: the shuffled letters are put inside the word for a baby-carriage

parts.note: a pram is a baby-carriage

indicators.note: possibly means the letters of the two words might be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: A child in a pram taking a route to a commander's tent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts ETORIU (the anagram of ROUTE I, from 'possibly') inside PRAM, between PRA and M.
explanation.definitionFit: In a Roman camp the commander's headquarters tent was the praetorium, named for the praetor or general.
